summary:
Earth Trend Globe is an interactive 3D globe that shows how Earth’s climate has changed since 1981. It also shows which of those changes are real.

We used 45 years of NASA POWER data (MERRA-2, CERES and GEWEX SRB) for six variables: temperature, humidity, rainfall, sunlight, air pollution and ozone. The data covers 16,020 points around the world. Users can click anywhere, choose a region, or draw their own area. Each area gets a trend per decade and a significance test that allows for month-to-month memory in the data. If a change isn’t clear yet, the app says how many more years of data it would need.

A “data detective” mode suggests places worth exploring. Live storms, floods and fires from NASA EONET are linked to the long-term trend at the same spot. A statistical outlook, tested on 2008 to 2025, shows what 2040 could look like for 184 areas.

This matters because a single heatwave or flood is easy to mistake for a trend. Our globe separates real change from natural ups and downs, and it explains everything in plain language. It is honest about what the data does and doesn’t show.
details:
Earth Trend Globe is an interactive 3D globe that shows how Earth’s climate has changed since 1981, and whether each change is real or just natural ups and downs.

  • Choose and explore. Users choose one of six variables: temperature, humidity, rainfall, sunlight, air pollution or ozone. They can spin the globe, click any point, pick a continent, country or region, or draw their own area. The globe is coloured by trend: red for rising, blue for falling, and a light grey veil where there’s no significant change.
  • Side panel. Opening a place shows:
    • a plain-English verdict and a chart of every month since 1981, with the trend line and a 95% confidence band;
    • the change per decade;
    • a month-by-month table comparing each month with a normal month of the same name.
  • How the statistics work.
    • Seasons are removed by comparing each month with its long-term average.
    • A trend line is fitted through what’s left.
    • The p-value allows for autocorrelation: one month tends to be like the month before, so 540 months may carry the information of far fewer independent ones. Without this correction, the app would claim false trends.
    • A Mann-Kendall test checks the result without assuming a straight line.
    • If a trend isn’t significant yet, the app estimates how many more years of data it would need.
  • Data detective. Users answer two questions, “what?” and “where?”. The app then ranks places by how clearly they are changing and gives a reason to look at each one.
  • Live NASA events. Storms, floods, fires and icebergs from NASA EONET appear on the globe. Opening one shows the long-term trend at that spot and a link to NASA Worldview for that place and day.
  • 2040 outlook.
    • For 184 areas, a statistical model projects 2,000 possible futures: the trend plus realistic year-to-year variation.
    • To check it, we hid 2008 to 2025, predicted those years from the earlier data, and compared the predictions with what really happened.
    • The model then picks whichever trend did better in that test: the whole record or only the last 20 years. It widens its ranges until 9 in 10 of the real years fall inside them.

Benefits

  • It separates single weather events from long-term change, which is the most common confusion in climate conversations.
  • It is honest about uncertainty. It says “not significant yet” instead of exaggerating.
  • It turns research-grade NASA data into something anyone can explore in seconds. No downloads, accounts or coding needed.
  • It runs in any browser, including on phones, and still works on poor Wi-Fi, because it keeps a saved copy of the events.

Intended impact

We want students, teachers, journalists and the public to be able to check climate claims for themselves, using NASA’s own data. They should come away understanding what a significant trend is, why one hot summer doesn’t prove a trend on its own, and how their own region is changing. Linking live events to long-term trends shows how NASA’s tools work together. EONET and Worldview show what is happening now, and the globe shows whether it fits a pattern.

Tools, languages and software

  • Data:
    • NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis, GEWEX SRB and CERES for sunlight), monthly from 1981 to 2025 on a 2° grid of 16,020 points;
    • NASA EONET for live events;
    • NASA Worldview links;
    • NASA Blue Marble and night-lights textures.
  • Languages: JavaScript (React), HTML, CSS, and Node.js scripts for the data pipeline.
  • Libraries: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, react-globe.gl (three.js/WebGL) and Plotly.js.
  • Hosting: GitHub, with GitHub Actions deploying automatically to GitHub Pages. There is no backend: everything is static files, so it’s fast and free to host.
  • Hardware: none. It runs in any web browser on a computer, tablet or phone.

How it is creative

  • Ask, don’t scroll. Instead of a static map, users ask questions: “Is this real?”, “Where should I look?”, “What could 2040 look like here?”. The app answers in plain language.
  • Live events plus history. It ties a live news event to 45 years of data, so users can see whether today’s storm or fire fits a long-term pattern.
  • Uncertainty you can see. Faint colours mean small trends, grey means not significant, and the bands widen in the projection.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific honesty.
    • Autocorrelation-aware tests stop us from claiming false trends.
    • The outlook was tested on past data.
    • Projections are always labelled as statistical, not a climate forecast.
    • Gaps in the records are respected: sunlight starts in 1984 and air pollution in 2001.
    • An area is only averaged when at least half of it has data.
  • Accessibility.
    • Colours are red and blue, never red and green.
    • The direction is always written in words, so colour isn’t the only signal.
    • All text is at least 14px, every number has units, and there’s full keyboard control.
  • Plain language. Everything is written for people who don’t study science, and a “How it works” section explains each method.
  • Reliability. It needs no account or key, has a saved copy for offline demos, and works on phones.
  • Transparency. The code is public on GitHub, and METHODS.md names every formula used.
